prompt: Quitanda sends every click with `partition_key` set to the customer's id. What does that guarantee?
hint: Think about where two clicks of one customer end up.

choices.text: Every partition receives the same share of clicks
choices.why: The key spreads load only as well as the keys hash; in the lesson two of four customers shared partition 3.

choices.text: Each shopper's taps share a partition and keep their order
choices.why: Right. The hash of the key picks one partition, and a partition keeps the order of what was appended to it.

choices.text: Clicks are read back in the order they happened across all customers
choices.why: Order holds inside a partition and nowhere else; across customers on different partitions it is gone.

choices.text: The producer is told which partition each click went to
choices.why: `send_event` returned nothing; the lesson had to ask the hub to find out.

prompt: After `send_clicks.py`, `partitions.py` reported partition 2 as `empty True`. Why?
hint: Count the keys and the partitions.

choices.text: The emulator keeps one partition in reserve for failover
choices.why: There is no reserve partition; every partition takes whatever keys hash to it.

choices.text: Partition 2 is for the `fraud` consumer group
choices.why: Consumer groups read every partition; partitions are not assigned to groups.

choices.text: Its events expired before the program asked
choices.why: Retention is a day or more, and nothing in the lesson waited that long.

choices.text: Four keys hashed to three partitions
choices.why: Right. `c-17` and `c-03` both hashed to partition 3, so one partition received none of the four keys.

prompt: A producer sends audit events that need no order at all. During a partition's maintenance, which way of sending keeps sends succeeding?
hint: A key, or a named partition, has exactly one place to go.

choices.text: With no key and no partition
choices.why: Right. The service then sends each event to a partition that is up; the price is that no order is kept, which these events do not need.

choices.text: With the audit id as the partition key, so events spread evenly
choices.why: Spread is not the problem; a keyed event has one partition to go to and waits or fails while it is down.

choices.text: With `partition_id` naming a partition chosen at random
choices.why: A named partition is one destination too; if it is the one under maintenance, the send waits or fails.

choices.text: With a constant key, so they all share one partition
choices.why: That ties every event to one partition, which is the worst case for both load and availability.

prompt: A Standard event hub was created with 4 partitions, and Quitanda now wants 8. What does the documentation say?
hint: The tier decides whether the count is fixed.

choices.text: It is fixed on Standard; growing it needs Premium, Dedicated or a new hub
choices.why: Right. Premium and Dedicated allow an increase, never a decrease; Basic and Standard do not change it after creation.

choices.text: It doubles itself when traffic grows, like auto-inflate
choices.why: Auto-inflate raises throughput units, which are capacity, not partitions.

choices.text: It is changed with one command, and every key stays on its partition
choices.why: Even where an increase is allowed, keys move to other partitions and their order across the change is lost.

choices.text: Partitions are per namespace, so adding a hub adds them
choices.why: Partitions belong to an event hub; capacity belongs to the namespace.

prompt: `read_clicks.py` read the ten clicks with `$Default`, and a second run read the same ten again. Why were they still there?
hint: What removes an event from a partition?

choices.text: A read removes nothing; retention does
choices.why: Right. Retention is the only deletion; a reader only chooses a position.

choices.text: The emulator does not delete read events, but Azure does
choices.why: Azure behaves the same way here: a read leaves the event in place for every other reader.

choices.text: The first run crashed before acknowledging them
choices.why: There is no acknowledgement in Event Hubs; the reader keeps its own position.

choices.text: `-1` tells the service to restore deleted events
choices.why: `-1` means the oldest event the partition still keeps; nothing had been deleted.

prompt: A reader stores "last sequence number read: 5" once for the whole `clicks` hub. What is wrong with that?
hint: Who numbers the events?

choices.text: Sequence numbers are reused after each checkpoint
choices.why: A partition never reuses a sequence number; checkpoints do not touch the numbering.

choices.text: Each partition numbers its own events, so 5 names a different event in each
choices.why: Right. Sequence number 5 on partition 3 and on partition 0 are unrelated; a position is per partition.

choices.text: It should store the offset, which is unique across the hub
choices.why: Offsets are per partition too; both partitions 0 and 3 had an event at offset 144.

choices.text: Nothing, if the hub has a single consumer group
choices.why: The number of groups is beside the point; the numbering is per partition.

prompt: Match each need to the `starting_position` that serves it.
hint: One of them is a time rather than a position.

pairs.left: Reprocess everything the retention still keeps
A live dashboard that ignores the past
Resume right after the last event handled
Replay since 09:00, after a bug fix

right_distractors: an offset of `0` for the whole hub

prompt: Quitanda's lake copy is stopped for nine days on a Standard hub whose retention is seven days. It restarts from its checkpoints. What happens?
hint: What exists in the partition when it asks?

choices.text: It reads all nine days, because checkpoints protect unread events
choices.why: A checkpoint is the reader's note; the service drops events at the end of the retention whether anybody read them or not.

choices.text: The hub refuses to start the reader until an operator resets it
choices.why: Nothing refuses: the reader starts and finds the oldest event the partition still keeps.

choices.text: It loses the two oldest days for good, with no error
choices.why: Right. Those events no longer exist; comparing the partition's first sequence number with the checkpoint is how a reader notices.

choices.text: It reads the last seven days twice
choices.why: Nothing is duplicated; the gap is at the start, not a repeat.

prompt: Quitanda's fraud check and its lake copy both read `clicks`. Why does each get a consumer group of its own?
hint: A group is a set of positions.

choices.text: So that each keeps its own position and sees every event
choices.why: Right. Sharing a group would make them split partitions, and each would miss what the other read.

choices.text: Because a group can only read two partitions
choices.why: A group reads every partition of the hub.

choices.text: So that the fraud check reads the events first and removes them
choices.why: Reading removes nothing, in any group.

choices.text: Because each group is billed separately and the lake copy is cheaper
choices.why: Groups are not billed one by one; what readers cost is the outgoing traffic they cause.

prompt: `python read_clicks.py analytics` printed nothing, with no error, while the hub held ten clicks. What does the lesson take from it?
hint: The emulator knows two groups.

choices.text: The group was created empty and starts at `@latest`
choices.why: No group was created; a reader naming a group does not create it, on Azure or here.

choices.text: A silent reader proves nothing; check the hub has events
choices.why: Right. Azure refuses a group that does not exist; this emulator answered silence, which looks like a quiet hub.

choices.text: `analytics` had already read the clicks earlier in the lesson
choices.why: No reader used that group before, and reading would not have removed anything anyway.

choices.text: Basic tier allows a single group
choices.why: True of Basic on Azure, but the emulator has no tiers, and it did accept `fraud`.

prompt: The fraud check runs as six copies in one consumer group on the four-partition `clicks` hub. What do the copies do?
hint: Within a group, one reader per partition is the recommendation.

choices.text: Each reads every partition, so every click is checked six times
choices.why: Copies in one group split the partitions; reading everything is what separate groups do.

choices.text: The service adds two partitions so that each copy has one
choices.why: The partition count is fixed at creation on Standard and is never changed by readers.

choices.text: They share each partition, a sixth of its events each
choices.why: A partition is not split between readers; a second reader on one partition receives every event of it.

choices.text: Four read a partition each and two wait for one to free up
choices.why: Right. The partition count is the ceiling on parallel readers in one group.

prompt: Where does a checkpoint live when a reader uses `BlobCheckpointStore`?
hint: The lesson listed it with `az storage blob list`.

choices.text: In the event hub, beside the partition
choices.why: Event Hubs does not remember readers' positions; the reader keeps them.

choices.text: In a blob's metadata, one blob per partition and group
choices.why: Right. `localhost/clicks/$default/checkpoint/3` carried the sequence number and offset in its metadata.

choices.text: In memory, so a restart starts at `starting_position` again
choices.why: The second run resumed after the checkpoint, which is the point of writing it to storage.

choices.text: In the event itself, as a property set by the reader
choices.why: Events cannot be changed after they are sent, and a reader writes nothing into the hub.

prompt: `checkpointed.py` ran with `starting_position` `-1`, read ten clicks, and on its second run read only the ten new ones. Why did `-1` not start it from the beginning again?
hint: Which wins when both exist?

choices.text: The first run deleted the clicks it had read
choices.why: Nothing was deleted: `read_clicks.py` would still read all twenty.

choices.text: `-1` means the end of the partition on a second run
choices.why: `-1` always means the oldest event kept; it was simply not used.

choices.text: Where a checkpoint exists, it wins
choices.why: Right. `starting_position` applies only to a partition with no checkpoint; partition 3 continued at sequence number 6.

choices.text: The service remembered the consumer group's last position
choices.why: The service remembers nothing about readers; the blob in Azurite did.

prompt: Quitanda's fraud check handles 600 clicks a second at the peak and checkpoints after every event. How many checkpoint writes to Blob Storage does it make in one peak hour?
hint: One write per event.

prompt: What does Event Hubs Capture write into storage?
hint: A row format that carries its schema.

choices.text: Avro files, a series per partition
choices.why: Right. Each record holds one event's body untouched, beside its sequence number, offset and enqueued time.

choices.text: Parquet files with one column per JSON field
choices.why: Event Hubs never looks inside the body, so it could not split JSON into columns; converting is a later job.

choices.text: One blob per event, named by its sequence number
choices.why: One blob per event would be millions of tiny files; Capture batches by a window.

choices.text: Delta tables
choices.why: Delta is a table format the lake lessons write with other tools; Capture's output is Avro.

prompt: `terraform validate` accepted `interval_in_seconds = 30` in the Capture block. What does that tell you?
hint: Where is the one-minute minimum enforced?

choices.text: Azure has lowered the minimum window to 30 seconds
choices.why: The documented time window is 1 to 15 minutes; validate does not read Azure's documentation.

choices.text: The rule is Azure's, checked at `apply`
choices.why: Right. `validate` checks what the schema encodes, such as the list of `sku` values, and asks Azure nothing.

choices.text: Capture rounds the value up to a minute on its own
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the value would be sent to Azure as written.

choices.text: The emulator would capture every 30 seconds
choices.why: The emulator has no Capture at all.

prompt: A Dedicated namespace is not a `sku` of `azurerm_eventhub_namespace`: Dedicated capacity is a resource of its own, a ___, that namespaces are placed on.
hint: The Terraform resource is `azurerm_eventhub_...`.

prompt: Why is the Basic tier ruled out for Quitanda's `clicks` before price is mentioned?
hint: Count the readers.

choices.text: Its retention of one day is too short for the lake copy
choices.why: One day is what the lesson's own declaration uses, because Capture keeps the lasting copy.

choices.text: One consumer group, for two readers
choices.why: Right. With `$Default` alone, the fraud check and the lake copy could not each keep a position.

choices.text: Basic hubs have no partitions, so no key could keep its clicks in order
choices.why: Basic hubs have partitions, up to 32.

choices.text: Basic events are limited to 64 KB
choices.why: 64 KB is the unit ingress events are counted in, not a tier's size limit.

prompt: A Standard namespace with auto-inflate went from 2 to 6 throughput units during a Friday promotion. On Monday nobody has touched it. What is it doing?
hint: Auto-inflate moves in one direction.

choices.text: Running at 2 units again, because auto-inflate scales back at midnight
choices.why: Auto-inflate does not lower units on its own; somebody or something has to.

choices.text: Throttling, because the promotion used up the month's units
choices.why: Units are a rate per second bought by the hour, not a monthly allowance.

choices.text: Still at 6, billed for 6 every hour, Capture included
choices.why: Right. The count stays high until lowered, and on Standard Capture is billed per unit too.

choices.text: Moved to Premium, where units are processing units
choices.why: Auto-inflate never changes the tier.

prompt: At the lesson's illustrative 0.03 USD per throughput unit-hour and 0.10 USD per unit-hour for Capture, what do 3 units with Capture cost for a 730-hour month, in USD?
hint: Both meters count unit-hours.

prompt: Put in order what happens to click 11 of the lesson, from the app to the second run of `checkpointed.py`.
hint: The checkpoint is written after the event is handled.
items: The hash of `c-17` puts it on partition 3, as sequence number 6
The reader finds the checkpoint at sequence number 5 and starts after it
`update_checkpoint` records sequence number 6 in the blob

prompt: Which of these did this lesson see the emulator do as Azure would? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what ran from what was only documented.

choices.text: Keep one key's events in one partition, in order
choices.why: Right; every `c-17` click landed on partition 3 in the order sent.

choices.text: Give two consumer groups the same events independently
choices.why: Right; `$Default` and `fraud` each read all ten.

choices.text: Refuse a consumer group that does not exist
choices.why: The emulator answered silence for `analytics`; the refusal is Azure's, documented and not run.

choices.text: Write Capture files into Azurite
choices.why: The emulator has no Capture; only the Terraform declaration was checked.

choices.text: Throttle a sender beyond one throughput unit
choices.why: The emulator has no units and accepted everything as fast as Python sent it.

prompt: A new team wants the click stream for a recommendations model, read once a night. Which plan fits what this lesson taught?
hint: Who already writes every click somewhere lasting?

choices.text: Read Capture's files in the lake
choices.why: Right. A nightly reader needs history, which the hub drops after a day; Capture already wrote it.

choices.text: Join the `fraud` consumer group so the hub sends nothing extra
choices.why: Sharing a group would split partitions with the fraud check, and each would miss events.

choices.text: Add a consumer group and read from `@latest` each night
choices.why: `@latest` reads only what arrives after it starts, so a nightly run would see almost nothing of the day.

choices.text: Raise retention to 90 days on the Standard hub
choices.why: Standard allows seven days at most, and a hub is not meant to be anybody's history.
